events.text:
📉🚢 Iran’s leverage in Hormuz bites as tanker traffic plunges
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has entered its most intense period of disruption since the start of the US-Israeli strikes on Iran, with 24 vessels hit in two weeks and six on Sunday alone, the Financial Times reported.
The pressure is showing in the numbers: only 2.9 million barrels of oil moved through the strait on October 11, while the seven-day average stood around 43% below pre-war levels.
Shipowners are increasingly avoiding the area, and some vessels have turned away from Gulf cargo hubs altogether.
Meanwhile, global supertanker earnings have surged to a record $805,000 per day as longer routes and ship-to-ship transfers disrupt normal flows.
Seven months into the war, Iran is still using the Strait of Hormuz as a powerful pressure point against vastly superior US military and economic power.

🇮🇱 Netanyahu pushes for another Iran war as elections loom
Benjamin Netanyahu has repeatedly discussed with Donald Trump the possibility of launching a new major US-Israeli operation against Iran before the Israeli and US elections, Axios reported.
The talks reportedly covered strikes on Iranian military and nuclear targets, while US and Israeli forces remain on alert and continue preparations.
💬 “Bibi seems to want to go in again,” a US official said, adding that Trump’s response has essentially been: “Go ahead and get ready.”
But another attack carries an obvious price. Israeli military officials reportedly expect Iran to retaliate with hundreds of ballistic missiles, potentially forcing Israel to postpone its October 27 election, while Washington fears renewed fighting could drive already high fuel prices even higher.
The White House officially denies Trump and Netanyahu discussed restarting the war, while Axios reports Trump has been wavering over whether to strike again.

events.text:
🇸🇦💥 Houthi missiles punch through Saudi air defenses as US-made interceptor stocks run low
Saudi Arabia has opened an investigation into how its air-defense network failed to stop recent Houthi missile and drone attacks on Riyadh, including the deadly strike on King Khalid International Airport, Associated Press reported. Investigators are examining both the interception failure and why weapons flying more than 1,000 km were not detected earlier.
AP noted that maneuvering Houthi ballistic missiles can pose a challenge to Patriot interceptors, while Al Jazeera reported that Saudi Arabia and other US allies are struggling with limited stocks of Patriot and THAAD munitions after heavy expenditure during the Iran war.
The Wall Street Journal, citing Saudi officials, separately reported that Riyadh is running low on interceptor missiles and has been moving air-defense batteries around the country to protect airports, energy infrastructure and palaces.
For all the billions poured into Western air defenses, Houthi missiles increasingly seem right at home in Saudi skies.
